Cognates Cognate with Scots day, dei, dey, dy (“day”), Yola daie, dei, dey, die (“day”), North Frisian dai, doi, däi (“day”), Saterland Frisian Dai (“day”), West Frisian dei (“day”), Bavarian Dåg, Tåg (“day”), Central Franconian Daach (“day”), Cimbrian tag, tage (“day”), Dutch dag, dagge (“day”), German Tag (“day”), German Low German Dag, Dagg (“day”), Limburgish Daach, Daag (“day”), Luxembourgish Dag (“day”), Mòcheno ta (“da…

senses.d: The time when the Sun is above the horizon and it lights the sky.
ex: day and night;  I work at night and sleep during the day.

senses.d: A period of time equal or almost equal to a full day-night cycle, being 24 hours long.
ex: I've been here for two days and a bit.

senses.d: The time taken for the Sun to seem to be in the same place in the sky twice; a solar day.
The time taken for the Earth to make a full rotation about its axis with respect to the fixed stars; a sidereal day or stellar day.
A 24-hour period beginning at 6am or sunrise.
ex: Your 8am forecast: The high for the day will be 30 and the low, before dawn, will be 10.

senses.d: A period of time between two set times which mark the beginning and the end of day in a calendar, such as from midnight to the following midnight or (Judaism) from nightfall to the following nightfall.
ex: The day begins at midnight.
Monday is the first day of the week in many countries of the world.

senses.d: The rotational period of a planet.
ex: A day on Mars is slightly over 24 hours.
Radio emissions indicate that a Neptunian day lasts 16.1 hours, an hour and a half shorter than previously thought.

senses.d: The part of a day period which one spends at one’s job, school, etc.
ex: I worked two days last week.

senses.d: An observance lasting for a day, such as an annual holiday.
ex: Christmas Day
Remembrance Day

senses.d: A day set aside for a specified activity.
ex: leg day, moving day, observation day

senses.d: To spend a day (in a place).
ex: I nighted and dayed in Damascus town[.]

grp.label: part of a day period which one spends at one's job, school, etc.
period from midnight to the following midnight

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dia, from Vulgar Latin *dia, first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs, reformed from the accusative diem, from Proto-Italic *djēm, the accusative of *djous (“day, sky”), from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Distantly related to Deus, Zeus and Jove.

chain.g: A solar or sidereal day of about 24 hours, especially (historical) Roman dates reckoned from one midnight to the next.

phr: a broken clock is right twice a day

ety.text: From Middle English dayes, dawes, from Old English dagas, from Proto-Germanic *dagōs, *dagōz, plural of *dagaz, equivalent to day + -s (plural ending).
From Middle English daies, from Old English dæġes (“by day”), from Proto-Germanic *dagas, *dagis, genitive of *dagaz, equivalent to day + -s (adverbial ending).

senses.d: A particular time or period of vague extent.
ex: Things were more relaxed in Grandpa's days.
His days of being the king are over.

senses.d: Life.
ex: That's how he ended his days.

senses.d: During the day.
ex: She works days at the garage.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vida, from Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā.

ety.text: From Middle English daye-lighte, dey liȝht, dailiȝt, day-liht, dai-liht (also as days lyȝt, daies liht), equivalent to day + light. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Deegeslucht, Daisljoacht (“daylight”), West Frisian deiljocht (“daylight”), Dutch daglicht (“daylight”), German Tageslicht (“daylight”).

senses.d: The natural light that is ambient in daytime, being mostly sunlight (both direct and indirect, on either sunny days or cloudy days).
ex: Meronym: sunbeams
Near-synonyms: sunlight, sunshine

senses.d: A light source that simulates daylight.
The intensity distribution of light over the visible spectrum generated by the Sun under various conditions or by other light sources intended to simulate natural daylight.
The period of time between sunrise and sunset.
ex: burning daylight
wasting daylight

senses.d: Daybreak.
ex: We had only two hours to work before daylight.
Towards the following morning, the thermometer fell to 5°; and at daylight, there was not an atom of water to be seen in any direction.

senses.d: Exposure to public scrutiny.
ex: Budgeting a spy organization can't very well be done in daylight.

senses.d: A clear, open space.
ex: All small running backs instinctively run to daylight.
He could barely see daylight through the complex clockwork.

senses.d: The space between platens on a press or similar machinery.
ex: The minimum and maximum daylights on an injection molding machine determines the sizes of the items it can make.

senses.d: Emotional or psychological distance between people, or disagreement.
ex: We completely agree. There's no daylight between us on the issue.

senses.d: Meaningful or noticeable difference or distinction between two things, especially concepts.
ex: There's not much daylight between saying that the universe is God and saying that God doesn't exist.

senses.d: To expose to daylight
ex: […] the Morlocks, subterranean for innumerable generations, had come at last to find the daylit surface intolerable.
[…] she was not looking at the daylit, sunny world which she so wanted to see.

senses.d: To provide sources of natural illumination such as skylights or windows.
To allow light in, as by opening drapes.
To run a drainage pipe to an opening from which its contents can drain away naturally.
To gain exposure to the open.
ex: The seam of coal daylighted at a cliff by the river.
Tunnels were enlarged or daylighted and clearances generally greatly improved.

senses.d: To moonlight (work a second, often illicit job) during the daytime.

grp.label: period of time between sunrise and sunset

Pertaining to daytime; appropriate to the day.
